statement: At 3:00 the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock are at right angles. How many minutes later are the two hands next at right angles?

choices.misconception: I worked out when the minute hand catches up with the hour hand, 90 / 5.5 minutes, instead of when it is 90 degrees past it.
I added the speeds of the hands, 6 + 0.5 = 6.5 degrees per minute, instead of subtracting them, and divided 180 by 6.5.
I ignored the movement of the hour hand, so I sent the minute hand to the 6, a quarter turn past the 3.
I used the gap between two moments when the hands lie on top of each other, as if right angles came that far apart.

hints: The hour hand starts a quarter turn ahead. Where must the minute hand reach?
The minute hand turns 6 degrees per minute and the hour hand half a degree, so it gains 5.5 degrees per minute. How many degrees must it gain to go from 90 behind the hour hand to 90 ahead?
The minute hand must gain 180 degrees at 5.5 degrees per minute.

solutions.reliable: At 3:00 the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand at 3, so the minute hand is 90 degrees behind. The minute hand turns 6 degrees per minute and the hour hand 0.5 degrees per minute, so the minute hand gains 5.5 degrees per minute. After it catches up, the next right angle comes when it is 90 degrees ahead, so in total it must gain 90 + 90 = 180 degrees. That takes 180 / 5.5 = 360 / 11 = 32 8/11 minutes, a little after 3:32. Check at that moment: the minute hand is at 6 x 360/11 = 196 4/11 degrees and the hour hand at 90 + 180/11 = 106 4/11 degrees, which differ by exactly 90. The transferable idea: treat the hands as runners, and turn each question about their angle into how much the faster hand must gain.
solutions.elegant: Right angles happen 44 times in 12 hours. Starting from the right angle at 3:00, the next one is half a lap of relative motion later, and a full lap of relative motion takes 720 / 11 minutes, so half a lap takes 360 / 11 = 32 8/11 minutes.

whyOnTest: Clock problems that ask when, not what angle, test the relative speed idea, and the traps are forgetting the hour hand moves or stopping at the moment the hands overlap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
